fields.name: AutoField
fields.description:
An `IntegerField` that automatically increments according to available
IDs. You usually won't need to use this directly; a primary key field will
automatically be added to your model if you don't specify otherwise. See
automatic-primary-key-fields.

`BigAutoField`
----------------

fields.name: BigAutoField
fields.description:
A 64-bit integer, much like an `AutoField` except that it is
guaranteed to fit numbers from `1` to `9223372036854775807`.

`BigIntegerField`
-------------------

fields.name: BigIntegerField
fields.description:
A 64-bit integer, much like an `IntegerField` except that it is
guaranteed to fit numbers from `-9223372036854775808` to
`9223372036854775807`. The default form widget for this field is a
`django.forms.NumberInput`.

`BinaryField`
---------------

fields.name: BinaryField
fields.description:
A field to store raw binary data. It can be assigned `bytes`,
`bytearray`, or `memoryview`.

By default, `BinaryField` sets `~Field.editable` to `False`, in which
case it can't be included in a `django.forms.ModelForm`.

arguments.name: max_length
arguments.description:
Optional. The maximum length (in bytes) of the field. The maximum length is
    enforced in Django's validation using
    `django.core.validators.MaxLengthValidator`.

fields.name: BooleanField
fields.description:
A true/false field.

The default form widget for this field is `django.forms.CheckboxInput`,
or `django.forms.NullBooleanSelect` if `null=True <Field.null>`.

The default value of `BooleanField` is `None` when `Field.default`
isn't defined.

`CompositePrimaryKey`
-----------------------

fields.name: CompositePrimaryKey
fields.description:
A virtual field used for defining a composite primary key.

This field must be defined as the model's `pk` attribute. If present, Django
will create the underlying model table with a composite primary key.

The `*field_names` argument is a list of positional field names that compose
the primary key.

See /topics/composite-primary-key for more details.

`CharField`
-------------

fields.name: CharField
fields.description:
A string field, for small- to large-sized strings.

For large amounts of text, use `django.db.models.TextField`.

The default form widget for this field is a `django.forms.TextInput`.

`CharField` has the following extra arguments:
fields.example:
If you are writing an application that must be portable to multiple
database backends, you should be aware that there are restrictions on
``max_length`` for some backends. Refer to the :doc:`database backend
notes </ref/databases>` for details.

arguments.name: max_length
arguments.description:
The maximum length (in characters) of the field. The `max_length`
    is enforced at the database level and in Django's validation using
    `django.core.validators.MaxLengthValidator`. It's required for all
    database backends included with Django except PostgreSQL and SQLite, which
    supports unlimited `VARCHAR` columns.

arguments.name: db_collation
arguments.description: Optional. The database collation name of the field.

fields.name: DateField
fields.description:
A date, represented in Python by a `datetime.date` instance. Has a few extra,
optional arguments:
fields.example:
As currently implemented, setting ``auto_now`` or ``auto_now_add`` to
``True`` will cause the field to have ``editable=False`` and ``blank=True``
set.

arguments.name: auto_now
arguments.description:
Automatically set the field to now every time the object is saved. Useful
    for "last-modified" timestamps. Note that the current date is *always*
    used; it's not just a default value that you can override.

arguments.name: auto_now_add
arguments.description:
Automatically set the field to now when the object is first created. Useful
    for creation of timestamps. Note that the current date is *always* used;
    it's not just a default value that you can override. So even if you
    set a value for this field when creating the object, it will be ignored.
    If you want to be able to modify this field, set the following instead of
    `auto_now_add=True`:

fields.name: DateTimeField
fields.description:
A date and time, represented in Python by a `datetime.datetime` instance.
Takes the same extra arguments as `DateField`.

The default form widget for this field is a single
`django.forms.DateTimeInput`. The admin uses two separate
`django.forms.TextInput` widgets with JavaScript shortcuts.


    If you have a `datetime.date` instance, it's recommended to convert it to
    a `datetime.datetime` first. If you don't, `DateTimeField` will
    use midnight in the default-current-time-zone for
    the time component. This is true for both storage and comparison. To
    compare the date portion of a `DateTimeField` with a
    `datetime.date` instance, use the `date` lookup.

`DecimalField`
----------------

fields.name: DecimalField
fields.description:
A fixed-precision decimal number, represented in Python by a
`decimal.Decimal` instance. It validates the input using
`django.core.validators.DecimalValidator`.

Has the following arguments:

arguments.name: max_digits
arguments.description:
The maximum number of digits allowed in the number. Note that this number
    must be greater than or equal to `decimal_places`. It's always required
    on MySQL because this database doesn't support numeric fields with no
    precision. It's also required for all database backends when
    `~DecimalField.decimal_places` is provided.

arguments.name: decimal_places
arguments.description:
The number of decimal places to store with the number. It's always required
    on MySQL because this database doesn't support numeric fields with no
    precision. It's also required for all database backends when
    `~DecimalField.max_digits` is provided.

fields.name: DurationField
fields.description:
A field for storing periods of time - modeled in Python by
`python:datetime.timedelta`. When used on PostgreSQL, the data type
used is an `interval` and on Oracle the data type is `INTERVAL DAY(9) TO
SECOND(6)`. Otherwise a `bigint` of microseconds is used.
fields.example:
Arithmetic with ``DurationField`` works in most cases. However on all
databases other than PostgreSQL, comparing the value of a ``DurationField``
to arithmetic on ``DateTimeField`` instances will not work as expected.

fields.name: EmailField
fields.description:
A `CharField` that checks that the value is a valid email address using
`django.core.validators.EmailValidator`.

`FileField`
-------------

fields.name: FileField
fields.description: A file-upload field.
fields.example:
The ``primary_key`` argument isn't supported and will raise an error if
used.

arguments.name: upload_to
arguments.description:
This attribute provides a way of setting the upload directory and file
    name, and can be set in two ways. In both cases, the value is passed to the
    `Storage.save() <django.core.files.storage.Storage.save>()` method.

arguments.name: storage
arguments.description:
A storage object, or a callable which returns a storage object. This
    handles the storage and retrieval of your files. See /topics/files
    for details on how to provide this object.

fields.name: FilePathField
fields.description:
A `CharField` whose choices are limited to the filenames in a certain
directory on the filesystem. Has some special arguments, of which the first is
**required**:

arguments.name: path
arguments.description:
Required. The absolute filesystem path to a directory from which this
    `FilePathField` should get its choices. Example: `"/home/images"`.

arguments.name: match
arguments.description:
Optional. A regular expression, as a string, that `FilePathField`
    will use to filter filenames. Note that the regex will be applied to the
    base filename, not the full path. Example: `"foo.*\.txt$"`, which will
    match a file called `foo23.txt` but not `bar.txt` or `foo23.png`.

arguments.name: recursive
arguments.description:
Optional. Either `True` or `False`. Default is `False`. Specifies
    whether all subdirectories of `~FilePathField.path` should be
    included

arguments.name: allow_files
arguments.description:
Optional. Either `True` or `False`. Default is `True`. Specifies
    whether files in the specified location should be included. Either this or
    `~FilePathField.allow_folders` must be `True`.

arguments.name: allow_folders
arguments.description:
Optional. Either `True` or `False`. Default is `False`. Specifies
    whether folders in the specified location should be included. Either this
    or `~FilePathField.allow_files` must be `True`.

fields.name: FloatField
fields.description:
A floating-point number represented in Python by a `float` instance.

The default form widget for this field is a `django.forms.NumberInput`
when `~django.forms.Field.localize` is `False` or
`django.forms.TextInput` otherwise.

.. _floatfield_vs_decimalfield:

fields.name: GeneratedField
fields.description:
A field that is always computed based on other fields in the model. This field
is managed and updated by the database itself. Uses the `GENERATED ALWAYS`
SQL syntax.

There are two kinds of generated columns: stored and virtual. A stored
generated column is computed when it is written (inserted or updated) and
occupies storage as if it were a regular column. A virtual generated column
occupies no storage and is computed when it is read. Thus, a virtual generated
column is similar to a view and a stored generated column is similar to a
materialized view.

arguments.name: expression
arguments.description:
An `Expression` used by the database to automatically set the field
    value each time the model is changed.

arguments.name: output_field
arguments.description: A model field instance to define the field's data type.

arguments.name: db_persist
arguments.description:
Determines if the database column should occupy storage as if it were a
    real column. If `False`, the column acts as a virtual column and does
    not occupy database storage space.

fields.name: GenericIPAddressField
fields.description:
An IPv4 or IPv6 address, in string format (e.g. `192.0.2.30` or
`2a02:42fe::4`). The default form widget for this field is a
`django.forms.TextInput`.

The IPv6 address normalization follows :rfc:`4291#section-2.2` section 2.2,
including using the IPv4 format suggested in paragraph 3 of that section, like
`::ffff:192.0.2.0`. For example, `2001:0::0:01` would be normalized to
`2001::1`, and `::ffff:0a0a:0a0a` to `::ffff:10.10.10.10`. All characters
are converted to lowercase.

arguments.name: protocol
arguments.description:
Limits valid inputs to the specified protocol.
    Accepted values are `'both'` (default), `'IPv4'`
    or `'IPv6'`. Matching is case insensitive.

arguments.name: unpack_ipv4
arguments.description:
Unpacks IPv4 mapped addresses like `::ffff:192.0.2.1`.
    If this option is enabled that address would be unpacked to
    `192.0.2.1`. Default is disabled. Can only be used
    when `protocol` is set to `'both'`.

fields.name: ImageField
fields.description:
Inherits all attributes and methods from `FileField`, but also
validates that the uploaded object is a valid image.

In addition to the special attributes that are available for
`FileField`, an `ImageField` also has `height` and `width`
attributes.

To facilitate querying on those attributes, `ImageField` has the
following optional arguments:

arguments.name: height_field
arguments.description:
Name of a model field which is auto-populated with the height of the image
    each time an image object is set.

arguments.name: width_field
arguments.description:
Name of a model field which is auto-populated with the width of the image
    each time an image object is set.

fields.name: IntegerField
fields.description:
An integer. Values are only allowed between certain (database-dependent)
points. Values from `-2147483648` to `2147483647` are compatible in all
databases supported by Django.

It uses `django.core.validators.MinValueValidator` and
`django.core.validators.MaxValueValidator` to validate the input based
on the values that the default database supports.

The default form widget for this field is a `django.forms.NumberInput`
when `~django.forms.Field.localize` is `False` or
`django.forms.TextInput` otherwise.

`JSONField`
-------------

fields.name: JSONField
fields.description:
A field for storing JSON encoded data. In Python the data is represented in its
Python native format: dictionaries, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and
`None`.

`JSONField` is supported on MariaDB, MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, and SQLite
(with the sqlite-json1).

arguments.name: encoder
arguments.description:
An optional `json.JSONEncoder` subclass to serialize data types
    not supported by the standard JSON serializer (e.g. `datetime.datetime`
    or `python:uuid.UUID`). For example, you can use the
    `django.core.serializers.json.DjangoJSONEncoder` class.

arguments.name: decoder
arguments.description:
An optional `json.JSONDecoder` subclass to deserialize the value
    retrieved from the database. The value will be in the format chosen by the
    custom encoder (most often a string). Your deserialization may need to
    account for the fact that you can't be certain of the input type. For
    example, you run the risk of returning a `datetime` that was actually a
    string that just happened to be in the same format chosen for
    `datetime`\s.

fields.name: PositiveBigIntegerField
fields.description:
Like a `PositiveIntegerField`, but only allows values under a certain
(database-dependent) point. Values from `0` to `9223372036854775807` are
compatible in all databases supported by Django.

`PositiveIntegerField`
------------------------

fields.name: PositiveIntegerField
fields.description:
Like an `IntegerField`, but must be either positive or zero (`0`).
Values are only allowed under a certain (database-dependent) point. Values from
`0` to `2147483647` are compatible in all databases supported by Django.
The value `0` is accepted for backward compatibility reasons.

`PositiveSmallIntegerField`
-----------------------------

fields.name: PositiveSmallIntegerField
fields.description:
Like a `PositiveIntegerField`, but only allows values under a certain
(database-dependent) point. Values from `0` to `32767` are compatible in
all databases supported by Django.

`SlugField`
-------------

fields.name: SlugField
fields.description:
:term:`Slug <slug>` is a newspaper term. A slug is a short label for something,
containing only letters, numbers, underscores or hyphens. They're generally
used in URLs.

Like a CharField, you can specify `~CharField.max_length` (read the note
about database portability and `~CharField.max_length` in that section,
too). If `~CharField.max_length` is not specified, Django will use a
default length of 50.

Implies setting `Field.db_index` to `True`.

It is often useful to automatically prepopulate a SlugField based on the value
of some other value. You can do this automatically in the admin using
`~django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin.prepopulated_fields`.

It uses `django.core.validators.validate_slug` or
`django.core.validators.validate_unicode_slug` for validation.

arguments.name: allow_unicode
arguments.description:
If `True`, the field accepts Unicode letters in addition to ASCII
    letters. Defaults to `False`.

fields.name: SmallAutoField
fields.description:
Like an `AutoField`, but only allows values under a certain
(database-dependent) limit. Values from `1` to `32767` are compatible in
all databases supported by Django.

`SmallIntegerField`
---------------------

fields.name: SmallIntegerField
fields.description:
Like an `IntegerField`, but only allows values under a certain
(database-dependent) point. Values from `-32768` to `32767` are compatible
in all databases supported by Django.

`TextField`
-------------

fields.name: TextField
fields.description:
A large text field. The default form widget for this field is a
`django.forms.Textarea`.

If you specify a `max_length` attribute, it will be reflected in the
`django.forms.Textarea` widget of the auto-generated form field.
However it is not enforced at the model or database level. Use a
`CharField` for that.
fields.example:
Collation names are not standardized. As such, this will not be
portable across multiple database backends.

arguments.name: db_collation
arguments.description: Optional. The database collation name of the field.

fields.name: TimeField
fields.description:
A time, represented in Python by a `datetime.time` instance. Accepts the same
auto-population options as `DateField`.

The default form widget for this field is a `django.forms.TimeInput`.
The admin adds some JavaScript shortcuts.

`URLField`
------------

fields.name: URLField
fields.description:
A `CharField` for a URL, validated by
`django.core.validators.URLValidator`.

The default form widget for this field is a `django.forms.URLInput`.

Like all `CharField` subclasses, `URLField` takes the optional
`~CharField.max_length` argument. If you don't specify
`~CharField.max_length`, a default of 200 is used.

`UUIDField`
-------------

fields.name: UUIDField
fields.description:
A field for storing universally unique identifiers. Uses Python's
`python:uuid.UUID` class. When used on PostgreSQL and MariaDB, this
stores in a `uuid` datatype, otherwise in a `char(32)`.

Universally unique identifiers are a good alternative to `AutoField` for
`~Field.primary_key`. The database will not generate the UUID for you, so
it is recommended to use `~Field.default`::

    import uuid
    from django.db import models


    class MyUUIDModel(models.Model):
        id = models.UUIDField(primary_key=True, default=uuid.uuid4, editable=False)
        # other fields

Note that a callable (with the parentheses omitted) is passed to `default`,
not an instance of `UUID`.
fields.example:
import uuid
from django.db import models


class MyUUIDModel(models.Model):
    id = models.UUIDField(primary_key=True, default=uuid.uuid4, editable=False)
    # other fields

fields.name: ForeignKey
fields.description:
A many-to-one relationship. Requires two positional arguments: the class to
which the model is related and the `~ForeignKey.on_delete` option::

    from django.db import models


    class Manufacturer(models.Model):
        name = models.TextField()


    class Car(models.Model):
        manufacturer = models.ForeignKey(Manufacturer, on_delete=models.CASCADE)

The first positional argument can be either a concrete model class or a
lazy-relationships to a model class.
recursive-relationships, where a model has a
relationship with itself, are also supported.

See `ForeignKey.on_delete` for details on the second positional
argument.

A database index is automatically created on the `ForeignKey`. You can
disable this by setting `~Field.db_index` to `False`. You may want to
avoid the overhead of an index if you are creating a foreign key for
consistency rather than joins, or if you will be creating an alternative index
like a partial or multiple column index.

Database Representation
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Behind the scenes, Django appends `"_id"` to the field name to create its
database column name. In the above example, the database table for the `Car`
model will have a `manufacturer_id` column. You can change this explicitly by
specifying `~Field.db_column`, however, your code should never have to
deal with the database column name (unless you write custom SQL). You'll always
deal with the field names of your model object.

.. _foreign-key-arguments:

Arguments
~~~~~~~~~

`ForeignKey` accepts other arguments that define the details of how the
relation works.

arguments.name: on_delete
arguments.description:
When an object referenced by a `ForeignKey` is deleted, the
    referring objects need updating. The `on_delete` argument specifies
    how this is done, and whether Django or your database makes the updates.
    For example, if you have a nullable `ForeignKey` and you want Django
    to set it to `None` when the referenced object is deleted::

arguments.name: limit_choices_to
arguments.description:
Sets a limit to the available choices for this field when this field is
    rendered using a `ModelForm` or the admin (by default, all objects
    in the queryset are available to choose). Either a dictionary, a
    `django.db.models.Q` object, or a callable returning a
    dictionary or `django.db.models.Q` object can be used.

arguments.name: related_name
arguments.description:
The name to use for the relation from the related object back to this one.
    It's also the default value for `related_query_name` (the name to use
    for the reverse filter name from the target model). See the backwards-related-objects for a full explanation
    and example. Note that you must set this value when defining relations on
    abstract-base-classes; and when you do so
    abstract-related-name is available.

arguments.name: related_query_name
arguments.description:
The name to use for the reverse filter name from the target model. It
    defaults to the value of `related_name` or
    `~django.db.models.Options.default_related_name` if set, otherwise it
    defaults to the name of the model::

arguments.name: to_field
arguments.description:
The field on the related object that the relation is to. By default, Django
    uses the primary key of the related object. If you reference a different
    field, that field must have `unique=True`.

arguments.name: db_constraint
arguments.description:
Controls whether or not a constraint should be created in the database for
    this foreign key. The default is `True`, and that's almost certainly what
    you want; setting this to `False` can be very bad for data integrity.
    That said, here are some scenarios where you might want to do this:

arguments.name: swappable
arguments.description:
Controls the migration framework's reaction if this `ForeignKey`
    is pointing at a swappable model. If it is `True` - the default -
    then if the `ForeignKey` is pointing at a model which matches
    the current value of `settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL` (or another swappable
    model setting) the relationship will be stored in the migration using
    a reference to the setting, not to the model directly.

fields.name: ManyToManyField
fields.description:
A many-to-many relationship. Requires a positional argument: the class to
which the model is related, which works exactly the same as it does for
`ForeignKey`, including recursive-relationships and
lazy-relationships relationships.

Related objects can be added, removed, or created with the field's
`django.db.models.fields.related.RelatedManager`.

Database Representation
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Behind the scenes, Django creates an intermediary join table to represent the
many-to-many relationship. By default, this table name is generated using the
name of the many-to-many field and the name of the table for the model that
contains it. Since some databases don't support table names above a certain
length, these table names will be automatically truncated and a uniqueness hash
will be used, e.g. `author_books_9cdf`. You can manually provide the name of
the join table using the `~ManyToManyField.db_table` option.

.. _manytomany-arguments:

Arguments
~~~~~~~~~

`ManyToManyField` accepts an extra set of arguments -- all optional --
that control how the relationship functions.

arguments.name: related_name
arguments.description: Same as `ForeignKey.related_name`.

arguments.name: related_query_name
arguments.description: Same as `ForeignKey.related_query_name`.

arguments.name: limit_choices_to
arguments.description: Same as `ForeignKey.limit_choices_to`.

arguments.name: symmetrical
arguments.description:
Only used in the definition of ManyToManyFields on self. Consider the
    following model::

arguments.name: through
arguments.description:
Django will automatically generate a table to manage many-to-many
    relationships. However, if you want to manually specify the intermediary
    table, you can use the `~ManyToManyField.through` option to specify
    the Django model that represents the intermediate table that you want to
    use.

arguments.name: through_fields
arguments.description:
Only used when a custom intermediary model is specified. Django will
    normally determine which fields of the intermediary model to use in order
    to establish a many-to-many relationship automatically. However,
    consider the following models::

arguments.name: db_table
arguments.description:
The name of the table to create for storing the many-to-many data. If this
    is not provided, Django will assume a default name based upon the names of:
    the table for the model defining the relationship and the name of the field
    itself.

arguments.name: db_constraint
arguments.description:
Controls whether or not constraints should be created in the database for
    the foreign keys in the intermediary table. The default is `True`, and
    that's almost certainly what you want; setting this to `False` can be
    very bad for data integrity. That said, here are some scenarios where you
    might want to do this:

arguments.name: swappable
arguments.description:
Controls the migration framework's reaction if this
    `ManyToManyField` is pointing at a swappable model. If it is
    `True` - the default - then if the `ManyToManyField` is pointing
    at a model which matches the current value of `settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL`
    (or another swappable model setting) the relationship will be stored in the
    migration using a reference to the setting, not to the model directly.

fields.name: OneToOneField
fields.description:
A one-to-one relationship. Conceptually, this is similar to a
`ForeignKey` with `unique=True <Field.unique>`, but the
"reverse" side of the relation will directly return a single object.

This is most useful as the primary key of a model which "extends"
another model in some way; multi-table-inheritance is
implemented by adding an implicit one-to-one relation from the child
model to the parent model, for example.

One positional argument is required: the class to which the model will be
related. This works exactly the same as it does for `ForeignKey`,
including all the options regarding recursive-relationships
and lazy-relationships relationships.

If you do not specify the `~ForeignKey.related_name` argument for the
`OneToOneField`, Django will use the lowercase name of the current model as
default value.

With the following example::

    from django.conf import settings
    from django.db import models


    class MySpecialUser(models.Model):
        user = models.OneToOneField(
            settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL,
            on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        )
        supervisor = models.OneToOneField(
            settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL,
            on_delete=models.CASCADE,
            related_name="supervisor_of",
        )

your resulting `User` model will have the following attributes:

.. code-block:: pycon

    >>> user = User.objects.get(pk=1)
    >>> hasattr(user, "myspecialuser")
    True
    >>> hasattr(user, "supervisor_of")
    True

A `RelatedObjectDoesNotExist` exception is raised when accessing the reverse
relationship if an entry in the related table doesn't exist. This is a subclass
of the target model's `Model.DoesNotExist
<django.db.models.Model.DoesNotExist>` exception and can be accessed as an
attribute of the reverse accessor. For example, if a user doesn't have a
supervisor designated by `MySpecialUser`::

    try:
        user.supervisor_of
    except User.supervisor_of.RelatedObjectDoesNotExist:
        pass

.. _onetoone-arguments:

Additionally, `OneToOneField` accepts all of the extra arguments
accepted by `ForeignKey`, plus one extra argument:
fields.example:
from django.conf import settings
from django.db import models


class MySpecialUser(models.Model):
    user = models.OneToOneField(
        settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL,
        on_delete=models.CASCADE,
    )
    supervisor = models.OneToOneField(
        settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL,
        on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name="supervisor_of",
    )

arguments.name: parent_link
arguments.description:
When `True` and used in a model which inherits from another
    :term:`concrete model`, indicates that this field should be used as the
    link back to the parent class, rather than the extra
    `OneToOneField` which would normally be implicitly created by
    subclassing.

common_options.name: null
common_options.description:
If `True`, Django will store empty values as `NULL` in the database.
Default is `False`.

common_options.name: blank
common_options.description: If `True`, the field is allowed to be blank. Default is `False`.

common_options.name: choices
common_options.description:
A mapping or iterable in the format described below to use as choices for this
field. If choices are given, they're enforced by
validating-objects and the default form widget will
be a select box with these choices instead of the standard text field.

common_options.name: db_column
common_options.description:
The name of the database column to use for this field. If this isn't given,
Django will use the field's name.

common_options.name: db_comment
common_options.description:
The comment on the database column to use for this field. It is useful for
documenting fields for individuals with direct database access who may not be

common_options.name: db_default
common_options.description:
The database-computed default value for this field. This can be a literal value
or a database function, such as `django.db.models.functions.Now`::

common_options.name: db_index
common_options.description: If `True`, a database index will be created for this field.

common_options.name: db_tablespace
common_options.description:
The name of the /topics/db/tablespaces to use for
this field's index, if this field is indexed. The default is the project's
`DEFAULT_INDEX_TABLESPACE` setting, if set, or the
`~Options.db_tablespace` of the model, if any. If the backend doesn't
support tablespaces for indexes, this option is ignored.

common_options.name: default
common_options.description:
The default value for the field. This can be a value or a callable object. If
callable it will be called every time a new object is created.

common_options.name: editable
common_options.description:
If `False`, the field will not be displayed in the admin or any other
`django.forms.ModelForm`. It will also be skipped during validating-objects. Default is `True`.

common_options.name: error_messages
common_options.description:
The `error_messages` argument lets you override the default messages that the
field will raise. Pass in a dictionary with keys matching the error messages
you want to override.

common_options.name: help_text
common_options.description:
Extra "help" text to be displayed with the form widget. It's useful for
documentation even if your field isn't used on a form.

common_options.name: primary_key
common_options.description: If `True`, this field is the primary key for the model.

common_options.name: unique
common_options.description: If `True`, this field must be unique throughout the table.

common_options.name: unique_for_date
common_options.description:
Set this to the name of a `DateField` or `DateTimeField` to
require that this field be unique for the value of the date field.

common_options.name: unique_for_month
common_options.description:
Like `~Field.unique_for_date`, but requires the field to be unique with
respect to the month.

common_options.name: verbose_name
common_options.description:
A human-readable name for the field. If the verbose name isn't given, Django
will automatically create it using the field's attribute name, converting
underscores to spaces. See verbose-field-names.

common_options.name: validators
common_options.description: A list of validators to run for this field. See the /ref/validators for more information.
